memory_lessons.applicability: Use as context for the larger partial-count experiment; it does not establish the best cap.
memory_lessons.claim: The fused candidate with a cap of 8192 partials was valid at 0.459449 ms versus the baseline's 1.228094 ms. It had zero correctness errors across 10 cases, including a maximum absolute error of 16 at the largest input; these results support fusion but do not establish that 8192 is optimal.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure the proposed 16384 cap against its parent on full-call time and all required correctness cases.

proposal.hypothesis: The previous fused candidate was correct and measured 0.459449 ms with up to 8192 partials. Keeping its approximate 4096-elements-per-partial policy but raising the cap to 16384 halves the large-input chunk size and doubles finalizer fan-in at the largest size. This tests whether more first-stage CTAs improve large-input parallelism enough to offset the more expensive finalizer; no speedup is assumed.

retained: Replace the two full-size absolute-value and atomic-sum passes with a fused first-stage sum(abs(x)) and one partial write per CTA.
Retain approximately 4096 input elements per partial, but raise the maximum partial count from 8192 to 16384; each CTA covers a contiguous input chunk with scalar loads.
Use a single 256-thread CUB finalizer to reduce all current-call partials and overwrite output; zero-length input explicitly overwrites output with zero.
